citeAs: Cheng, G., Han, J., & Lu, X. (2017). Remote Sensing Image Scene Classification: Benchmark and State of the Art. Proceedings of the IEEE.
creator: Gong Cheng, Junwei Han, Xiaoqiang Lu (Northwestern Polytechnical University)
description: NWPU-RESISC45 is a large-scale benchmark dataset for Remote Sensing Image Scene Classification (RESISC), created by Northwestern Polytechnical University (NWPU). It contains 31,500 images covering 45 scene classes with 700 images per class, each of size 256×256 pixels in RGB color space. The dataset features rich image variations in translation, spatial resolution, viewpoint, object pose, illumination, background, and occlusion, and covers more than 100 countries and regions worldwide.
name: NWPU-RESISC45
rai:annotatorDemographics: Experts in the field of remote sensing image interpretation (specific demographics not further described).
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Scene classes were selected in two steps: (1) investigating all scene classes of existing datasets to form 30 widely-used scene categories; (2) searching keywords related to OBIA, GEOBIA, land cover/use classification, geographic image retrieval, and geospatial object detection on Web of Science and Google Scholar to carefully select 15 additional meaningful scene classes, resulting in 45 total scene classes. Images were extracted and labeled by experts in the field of remote sensing image interpretation.
rai:dataBiases: The dataset was designed to address limitations of prior datasets including small scale, lack of image variations and diversity, and saturation of accuracy. To mitigate these biases, images were collected under all kinds of weathers, seasons, illumination conditions, imaging conditions, and scales, and fine-grained scene classes with high semantic overlapping were included (e.g., circular farmland vs. rectangular farmland, commercial area vs. industrial area, basketball court vs. tennis court). The dataset covers more than 100 countries and regions worldwide to ensure geographic diversity.
rai:dataCollection: Images were extracted by experts in the field of remote sensing image interpretation from Google Earth (Google Inc.), which maps the Earth by superimposition of images obtained from satellite imagery, aerial photography, and geographic information system (GIS) onto a 3D globe. The 31,500 images cover more than 100 countries and regions all over the world, including developing, transition, and highly developed economies. Images were carefully selected under all kinds of weathers, seasons, illumination conditions, imaging conditions, and scales.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Satellite imagery, aerial photography, and geographic information system (GIS) data accessed via Google Earth (Google Inc.). Images span spatial resolutions from approximately 30 m to 0.2 m per pixel for most scene classes.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset relies solely on overhead/satellite imagery and does not incorporate ground-level photos or social media data. The authors note that combining remote sensing data with information from social media and spatial technology could further improve scene classification. Some scene classes (island, lake, mountain, and snowberg) have lower spatial resolutions than the stated range of ~30 m to 0.2 m per pixel.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset enables the development and evaluation of new data-driven algorithms for remote sensing image scene classification, supporting applications such as natural hazards detection, land use and land cover determination, environment monitoring, and urban planning. By providing a large-scale publicly available benchmark, it facilitates advances in intelligent earth observation.
rai:dataUseCases: Remote sensing image scene classification; development and evaluation of data-driven algorithms including deep learning-based methods; land use and land cover (LULC) determination; natural hazards detection; geospatial object detection; geographic image retrieval; vegetation mapping; environment monitoring; urban planning.
